title: Stack vs Heap and Garbage Collection
oneLiner: Step through a C# program and watch frames push and pop, value types copy, references share one object, and the garbage collector find what nothing can reach.
keyTakeaway: Each thread's stack holds call frames with their locals and is freed instantly when a method returns. Objects created with new from a class live on the shared heap, and a variable holds only a reference to them. Assigning a struct copies its fields; assigning a class reference makes two names for one object. The garbage collector frees heap objects that no root (a live local, a static, a CPU register) can reach, and .NET's generational GC makes that cheap by collecting young objects most often.
explanation:
Every thread has a stack: a contiguous block of memory (1 MB by default on Windows, typically 8 MB for the main thread on Linux) where each method call pushes a frame holding its parameters, local variables and return address (where to carry on in the caller afterwards). When the method returns, its frame is popped by moving one pointer (a value holding a memory address), so stack allocation and freeing are essentially free. The stack is also why deep recursion (a method calling itself, thousands of levels deep) throws StackOverflowException: the frames simply run out of room.

The heap is one big shared region where objects with a lifetime that is not tied to a single method call live. In C#, new on a class (a reference type: string, List<T>, arrays, your own classes) allocates the object on the heap, and the variable holds a reference, effectively the object's address. Structs and the built-in numeric types are value types: the variable holds the value itself. So Point q = p; copies every field, and changing q leaves p alone, while Node b = a; copies only the reference, so b.Value = 11 changes the object a sees too. Step through the program below to see both.

"Value types live on the stack" is a common oversimplification that interviewers enjoy probing. A value type lives wherever its container lives: a struct local is in the stack frame, but a struct field of a class object, or the elements of an int[], are on the heap inside that object. Locals captured by a lambda (a small inline function), or kept across an await, are moved to a heap object as well. Boxing (assigning an int to an object variable) copies the value into a new heap object.

Nothing in C# frees heap memory explicitly. The garbage collector does it by tracing: starting from the roots (locals and parameters in every thread's live frames, static fields, CPU registers), it marks every object it can reach by following references, and everything left unmarked is garbage. Then it sweeps the dead space and, in .NET, usually compacts the survivors together so new allocations stay a fast pointer bump. Reference counting, used by Python and Swift, frees an object the moment its count drops to zero, but cannot by itself free two objects that refer to each other; tracing handles cycles naturally, because reachability is all that matters.

Tracing a big heap is expensive, so .NET's GC is generational, built on the observation that most objects die young. New objects go in generation 0, which is collected often and quickly. Survivors are promoted to gen 1, and survivors of that to gen 2, which is collected rarely. Objects of 85,000 bytes or more go straight to the Large Object Heap, which is collected with gen 2. A memory leak in a garbage collected language is therefore not forgotten frees; it is something still reachable that you no longer need, such as an ever-growing static cache or an event handler that is never unsubscribed. For unmanaged resources (files, sockets), the GC is too late and too unpredictable: that is what IDisposable and using are for.
